content:
Hey everyone!

I don't know many of you, so maybe I should introduce myself. I'm a PhD student at Caltech in the math department. I do mathematical physics but in practice that actually means a lot of higher category theory and operator algebras (the same sort of stuff Kim Morrison was doing before she started doing this). I've been thinking a lot about Lean the last couple of months and I saw some things that I find worrying. I decided to write up my thoughts in a little LessWrong post. I'm putting it here because I'm really curious about your thoughts; I probably have some misconceptions and I think this is an important topic to get right.

The name of the LessWrong post is "A critical look at Lean4".

Link: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/zHhGa3iQBQcdSifFL/a-critical-look-at-lean4-1
I don't claim you suggested this, but just to be clear I am not affiliated with/don't speak for Lean or the FRO. Also small correction, Mario's last name is Carneiro, not Carnerio.

Chris Bailey said:

I don't claim you suggested this, but just to be clear I am not affiliated with/don't speak for Lean or the FRO. Also small correction, Mario's last name is Carneiro, not Carnerio.

Thanks for replying! The part of the post where I quote you was definitely part of the reason I wanted to post this on Zulip. What I wrote in the article is "What was the Lean community's reaction to 'soundness bug #14576'? There's a nice thread about it on a Lean developer's forum", so hopefully that was clear enough that people understand you're just a contibutor of a forum and not part of the FRO. If anyone here thinks I took their words out of context or misrepresented the views of the dev community I'm happy to change the article

I think this needs some qualification upfront (as opposed to later in the post).

As of writing, there is no publicly available proof that Lean4 is consistent with respect to ZFC + any large cardinal axiom.

There is #leantt but it doesn't cover all features of lean, and there are some features like nested inductive types for which the relevant theorists are still building theory.

Does #leantt really to be mentioned immediately? I think the appropriate qualification is that I said "Lean4" instead of saying "Lean". I mention #leantt four paragraphs later (I call it "Mario Carneiro's Lean3 proof"). I also didn't feel the need to mention it earlier because Mario later found a serious flaw in his proof and my understanding is that this flaw has yet to be resolved.

yes indeed. Overall as a lean practitioner, I don't think any of these soundness issues would have cropped up in code that I handwrote or even incrementally used AI to formalize, unless the underlying libraries like mathlib or cslib relied on the unsoundness. So I probably perceive these soundness issues less seriously than those who rely on autoformalization; and consequently find the article's sentiment too strong. There is also ongoing work on the #lean4lean channel and they might be able to say more on what's happening w.r.t verifying lean's kernel.

Some thoughts.

  • We don't have a model for C++, how would you propose to prove the correctness of the official kernel? (You still need a human to check that the Lean translation is accurate with respect to the C++ code)
  • I don't get what's your point in the FLT comparator. Surely it isn't all that difficult for someone to rerun it with sandbox on? Or am I misunderstanding what the sandbox is?
  • The point of “proving consistency of con-leche doesn't say anything about bugs in official kernel” is true, but if one is paranoid, just double check everything with con-leche?
  • What would satisfy you? (Perhaps have a team of human cleaning up and understanding the proof of consistency of con-leche?)

user202729 said:

  • We don't have a model for C++, how would you propose to prove the correctness of the official kernel? (You still need a human to check that the Lean translation is accurate with respect to the C++ code)

I tried to make this point clear by saying that we don't have a high level understanding that Lean4 is consistent. The thing I was calling an open problem is the metamathematical question of why Lean4 is consistent. We do have a model for how Lean4's type theory is supposed to be defined and how it is supposed to behave, and as such we can prove things about it, just like #leantt tried to prove Lean3's consistency. It's the sort of thing that expert humans should be able to read and understand, and which can be treated not only as a certificate but as a guide for future work (this is the point I was making about how a theoretical understanding of Lean4's foundations would help bug-check the subtle parts of the kernel).

user202729 said:

  • I don't get what's your point in the FLT comparator. Surely it isn't all that difficult for someone to rerun it with sandbox on? Or am I misunderstanding what the sandbox is?

Yes, it's not difficult to re-run with the sandbox on. I added a footnote to clarify that I have personally re-ran it with the sandbox on, and so has Kevin Buzzard. The point I was making is that the fact that the sandbox was disabled and that Anthropic said they were treating their agent's Lean certificate as trusted is worrying to me. Sometimes when I bring this up to people they say "why does it matter that Anthropic treated their certificate as trusted? Isn't the whole point of Lean that you don't have to trust the person who made the proof?"

I decided to put this grievance in the context of Lean4's safety issues both to try to help AI safety people understand why you should enable your sandboxes, and to help Lean4 people understand the way their tool is being used.

user202729 said:

  • The point of “proving consistency of con-leche doesn't say anything about bugs in official kernel” is true, but if one is paranoid, just double check everything with con-leche?

Well, let me re-use the same quote about con-leche that I used in the article: "[Con-leche] does not need some of the hard-to-prove metatheoretical properties of Lean". Con-leche deliberately modified its kernel so that it throws up its hands when try to probe it with the subtle aspects of Lean4's type theory. The con-leche proof strategy does not directly translate to Lean4; I've tried this with Astra and it kept failing.

It's important to note that the solution is not "re-run everything in con-leche". Because there are examples of statements that compile in the official kernel but non con-leche, I imagine that major groups will run into the following issue. They will have developed their huge lean proof using the official kernel, and will want to get extra assurance by running it in con-leche. But then the con-leche won't accept their statement! This means that they will have to go through their entire work and try to fix it to make con-leche accept it as well. Maybe you think that every large-scale project should include con-leche during the entire development process and modify all their proofs so that con-leche accepts them, but that seems to not be the spirit of what con-leche is about and certainly this is not the default future we are headed towards.

user202729 said:

Some thoughts.

  • What would satisfy you? (Perhaps have a team of human cleaning up and understanding the proof of consistency of con-leche?)

To get an idea of what would satisfy me, I'd like to reproduce this quote from an openwall post (https://openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/08/02/1):

"Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408), the international standard used by
governments and defense organizations worldwide to certify security
products, defines formal verification as its highest assurance level.
EAL5 through EAL7 -- the levels required for national security systems,
cryptographic modules, smart card operating systems, separation kernels,
and avionics -- require semiformal or fully formal design verification.
EAL7 specifically demands mathematical proof of correspondence between
specification and implementation. Theorem provers like Lean 4 are among
the tools capable of producing these proofs."

I agree with Lean4's classification as EAL7 insofar as it relates to proofs that humans understand and are translated into Lean4 (possibly with AI assistance). I do NOT think that Lean4 certificates generated by agent swarms that just pass a "lake check" command should be treated as EAL7.

So I would be satisfied by either

(1) A change in the way Lean4's security is treated by frontier labs, tech companies developing formal verification for critical systems, and by governments

(2) A series advances in our theoretical and practical confidence in Lean4's security, as outlined in the "Where do we go from here?" part of my post

Milo Moses schrieb:

Because there are examples of statements that compile in the official kernel but non con-leche

What examples do you think of, and they from the “output of the Lean elaborator on realistic lean code” fragment, or the “constructed corner cases” fragment?

Maybe you think that every large-scale project should include con-leche during the entire development process and modify all their proofs so that con-leche accepts them, but that seems to not be the spirit of what con-leche is about and certainly this is not the default future we are headed towards.

Quote so! con-leche ships with lean-4.35 and lean check --paranoid runs it. I fully expect that everyone who has to worry about untrustworthy proofs will use con-leche and con-ron next to official, nanoda and lean4lean.

con-leche ships with lean-4.35

Wait, we're not including code that nobody understands into the Lean kernel (!), are we?
No, but it comes with the toolchain and is run as part of lake check --paranoid as an external checker.

And “code that nobody understands” is an unfair misrepresentation. I have been intensively working on con-leche for a while now. Yes, with a heavy agentic workflow, so there is understanding, conceptual and maybe a bit high-level. Yes, I did not write or even read every single line of code. But I have heavily discussed the design and the goal, set and revised them, worked on the proof, including distilling the core idea, and found, investigated and ruled on a number of (completeness, not soundness, of course) bugs. I wasn’t the programmer, but I am still the architect.

Joachim Breitner said:

What examples do you think of, and they from the “output of the Lean elaborator on realistic lean code” fragment, or the “constructed corner cases” fragment?

I don't really understand these examples myself. My Astra came up with them in the process of translating the con-leche proof into a proof that the official kernel is consistent. Here's a codeblock which it claims is a minimal example:

def P : Prop := ∀ A : Prop, A → A

local notation "δ" => (fun z : P => z (P → P) (fun x => x) z)
local notation "Ω" =>
  (δ (fun (A : Prop) (a : A) =>
    @Eq.rec Prop (P → P)
      (fun (B : Prop) (_ : (P → P) = B) => B)
      δ A (propext (Iff.intro (fun _ => a) (fun _ x => x)))))
local notation "ι" => (fun (A : Prop) (a : A) => a)
local notation "E" =>
  ((fun f : ∀ p q : P, p = q =>
    (fun _ : Ω = ι => True.intro) (f Ω ι))
    (fun p q : P => Eq.refl p))

theorem demo : E = True.intro := Eq.refl E
#print axioms demo

I don't know enough about Lean to say if these would come up on realistic code fragments, or just constructed corner cases. I've only ever worked on small-scale proofs that don't probe the unique features of Lean4.

EAL7 specifically demands mathematical proof of correspondence between specification and implementation. Theorem provers like Lean 4 are among the tools capable of producing these proofs.

Remark: Likely this was written before AI era and assume that the proof must obviously be written (and thus understood) by a human. In this age, “understood by a human” should be explicitly qualified in.

the fact that the sandbox was disabled and that Anthropic said they were treating their agent's Lean certificate as trusted is worrying to me.

For the record, the comment you quoted…

Comparator's own scripts/fake-landrun.sh is used = no sandbox, which is how the recorded run was made; the sandbox guards against an untrusted solution, which is moot when you built the tree yourself.

is likely written by Claude, not Anthropic.

Still, I think the message you want to send is:

  1. apart from wiping files in your computer, the sandbox also prevent a solution from tampering with the comparator to make it falsely accept an incorrect proof. (May be more impactful if you actually demo such code instead of just claiming so)
  2. therefore, certificates should be verified with sandbox on.

On the other hand, one has to ask what “recorded run” refers to here.

Yeah, I suspect that the comment was written by Claude too. In my mind this is much scarier - you've let the AI agents decide how much verification their proofs should get, and they have decided for themselves that treating their work as untrusted is "moot"!

I also don't know what "recorded run" refers to. The Anthropic FLT proof is a bit of a slop piece, and that shows up in the hard-to-parse comments.
On a side note, I suspect they're making the agents using a “compact” form of English internally for token/thinking efficiency. (Given that math is harder than English, this seems sensible enough)

Milo Moses schrieb:

I don't know enough about Lean to say if these would come up on realistic code fragments, or just constructed corner cases. I

That looks very much like a constructed corner case, with a non-normalizing proof term (omega). You can discern most independent checkers by putting such terms in one place or another. The fact that lean has non-normalizing reduction is well known (and even if it didn't, you can have a arbitrary expensive “reduction mines” and probe the various checker’s reduction strategies that way.

And yes, this does and can lead to valid proofs accepted by one checker and rejected by another, but this is not new with con-leche (e.g. https://github.com/ammkrn/nanoda_lib/issues/44).

And the upcoming refinements to Lean4’s logic (lean4#14977) will make that issue less relevant, because after that, a checker should never have a reason to reduce a proof (a term of a prop), including omega. con-leche anticipates some of these logic changes already, and I can change the lines in defeq checking a bit (proof irrelevance before whnfCore) to make it more robust. So thanks for the example, I guess.

@Joachim Breitner Right, the example does seem a bit trivial. Here's another one (also generated by Astra):

import Lean

def sumTo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  Nat.lt_wfRel.wf.fix (fun n rec =>
    if h : n = 0 then 0 else
      n + rec (n - 1)
        (Nat.sub_lt (Nat.pos_of_ne_zero h) (by decide))) n

theorem sumTo_ten : sumTo 10 = 55 := by
  decide +kernel

#print axioms sumTo_ten
-- 'sumTo_ten' does not depend on any axioms

The reason con-leche doesn't accept this one has more to do with specific features of con-leche. Namely: the official kernel unfolds theorem bodies during this calculation, but con-leche deliberately keeps them opaque, so the calculation gets stuck.

Again, this is con-leche anticipating planned changes to lean (that have already been performed in the elaborator, which since a good while no longer relies on Acc.rec reduction for well-founded recursion)
But yes, the set of accepted proof isn't identical between all the various checkers out there, hence the corner-case section on the Kernel Arena. Some people are more bothered by this than others.

I am 90% sure that, in the current version of Lean4 on Github, there exists a proof of the statement "True=False" that would be accepted in such a way that the Lean community would call it a bug in need of patching.

I am 2% certain that we will soon be putting huge amounts of trust into Lean4 certificates produced by misaligned AIs, and that the human work we do as a community thinking about and fixing Lean4 in the next 24 months would fall under Less Wrong's classification of a pivotal act.

90% seems too low for the True=False claim. @Martin Dvořák has a repo documenting that almost all previous releases of the official Lean kernel have had such soundness issues. I see no reason to expect that 4.35 is any different.

Similarly, I would assume the 2% number should also be much higher. In fact, I'd argue huge amounts of trust is already being placed in Lean certificates with the recent OpenAI results.

Personally, I think focusing too much on soundness is a bit of a red herring. The right question is not "is the current release of Lean sound" but rather "can we eventually refine the Lean kernel into something that is sound without fundamentally changing Mathlib and other downstream uses." I'd be most interested to hear your epistemic odds that the practical Lean type theory (meaning, the core language features that 99% of users actually interact with, which are shared by Nanoda, con-leche, official kernel) is deeply unsound in a way that can not be repaired. Those are the odds that are most relevant.

Fixing Lean4's safety issues counts as a cybersecurity task, and as such (in my experience), Astra will refrain from answering questions. Astra was happy to try to prove that Lean4 was consistent, but when I asked it to take seriously the possibility that Lean4 is not consistent it shut down the chat as cybersecurity.

I think this is a very valuable point to emphasize. I've encountered similar "guardrail" issues when trying to use AI models to find bugs in Lean proofs and tools. Frontier labs need to start making a more nuanced distinction between defense and offensive cybersecurity work. Obviously, we don't want people using ChatGPT to hack the entire internet, but using AI to find bugs in Lean and Lean projects helps make everyone more secure.

I don't understand the lean4-soundness repository personally. It doesn't seem like it should be indication of the likelihood of the kernel having or not having further issues purely based on it having lots of versions on it. It represents what I would have thought to be a somewhat "trivial" property of software that when you find a bug in it, usually it applies to all versions before the one you found it in going back to when the thing the bug is in was added -- and this is a good sign that lots of versions are on it and that it's not that the kernel is changing every so often and so some new bug creeps in when someone changes one thing or another. So far when you find a new one you basically find one in all versions.

To me "all kernel versions before have had issues so we expect we still do" seems like a defensible position (though estimating how likely seems like it should have to do with how hard it's been to find the last one compared to previously?) but "look at how many versions had them" is no stronger, I expect I'd be more surprised if that list wasn't near complete.

I don't think "huge amounts of trust" is about verification of mathematical results; it might be more to do with things such as "it's proven impossible to escape this sandbox to access the internet, so we can do a full test inside the sandbox of just how much this AI (with all cybersecurity restrictions disabled) could hack into if it did escape - where the AI doing the proof of the sandbox knows or suspects that it's the same AI that will be constrained inside the sandbox later". Maybe people aren't doing that kind of proof right now, but it's not ridiculous to try proving such cybersecurity properties as a way to protect against certain AI misalignments.
I've seen several discussions about formal verification of sandboxes in the last few months, it's definitely on folks' radar.

@Jack McCarthy “deeply unsound in a way that can not be repaired” — what do you mean by this? The practical part is a subset of what con-leche support right? (Since, if I recalled correctly, mathlib compiles in con-leche?)

Chris Henson said:
